taxonomyNote: NatureServe treats Hypsiglena chlorophaea and H. ochrorhyncha as separate species following Mulcahy (2008), who split the former H. torquata; Colorado Parks and Wildlife lists the Colorado animals as H. jani and H. chlorophaea, and Idaho Fish and Game lists several H. torquata names under chlorophaea.
fieldMarks: Smooth scales and many dark blotches above, the largest and most conspicuous on the neck (CPW).
Pupil vertically elongate, like a cat's; 19-21 scale rows at midbody; divided anal scale (CPW).
Extra scale in front of the eye behind the nostril separates it from the Chihuahuan nightsnake (CPW).
Maximum about 62 cm (24 in) total length (CPW).
behavior: Exclusively nocturnal and rarely seen; mildly venomous but not dangerous to humans (CPW).
Spends most of its time under rocks, in crevices or in rodent burrows; found under rocks mainly in mild weather of spring, late summer and fall (CPW).
Eats mainly lizards and lizard eggs, sometimes small snakes, frogs, insects and salamanders (NatureServe; CPW).
habitat: Arid and semiarid plains, canyons and hillsides, usually rocky, dissected terrain with sandy or gravelly soil, including desert, grassland, shrubland and woodland (NatureServe; CPW).
range: South-central British Columbia south through Washington, Oregon, southern Idaho, eastern California, Nevada, Utah and western Colorado to Arizona, northeastern Baja California and northwestern mainland Mexico (NatureServe).

lookalikes.name: Chihuahuan nightsnake
lookalikes.howToTell: Lacks the extra scale in front of the eye, behind the nostril (CPW).
